Building a tide clock from spare parts

A tide clock shows how far the sea is through its cycle instead of the hour of the day. Mine is built from an old quartz movement, a slowed-down gear train and a hand-painted dial. This post walks through the parts, the wiring and the small program that keeps it honest.

Parts list

  1. A quartz clock movement with a seconds output
  2. A gear train with these stages:
    • a 12:1 reduction from the movement
    • a 1.035:1 correction stage
  3. A dial painted with high and low water marks

The correction stage is the only tricky part. Lunar tides repeat roughly every twelve hours and twenty-five minutes, so an ordinary clock drifts by almost an hour a day.

The control program

The microcontroller pulses the movement with pulse_coil() once per adjusted second and stores the offset in EEPROM so a power cut does not lose the phase.

def adjusted_seconds(now):
    period = 44714  # seconds in a mean tidal cycle
    return (now * 43200) // period

while True:
    pulse_coil()

Calibration takes one high tide: set the hand to the top of the dial when the water is at its highest and press the button.

Measured drift

WeekDrift (minutes)

The drift stays within a few minutes, which is far better than the tide tables can promise for a small harbour anyway.

A verse for the dial

Time and tide wait for no one,
but the clock will wait for both,
and the sea will keep its own count.

That rhyme is now painted around the edge of the dial, in letters small enough that visitors have to lean in to read it, which is rather the point of a clock that only tells you about the sea.
